title: Memorizing changes in the factory and using melody
summary: He learned changes on index cards at factory jobs and advises soloists to draw on the melody.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I don’t know if you can answer this but if you were playing an extended solo with Elvin Jones’ trio, what is going through your head? Are you thinking harmonically? That’s my question.

No I know all the changes. When I learn a tune I have to know everything that’s going on that there needs to be. Do I hear it at first? Maybe not. When I first learned how to memorize in blocks, when I was working in the factories, that’s how I learned my tunes. I used to work for Mohawk Tires and I worked for the canning factory in Mount Morris where I had to load pallets, stack pallets up with boxes six feet high and then ring the buzzer for the forklift, and the next stack. So I’d do this all day long. So I would bring my tune in, and I had a tune on an index card with the changes all written out. And I’d tack it up to the post that was right next to me, and as the boxes came down I’m going G minor seventh, C minor seventh. And by the time I got home at night I knew the changes like I learned poetry. Because I had a great English teacher who taught me how to memorize poems. And so I learned them. But I didn’t hear them. Now I get home, I know all the changes and don’t have to look at a book. I know the melody and now I start looking at the melody and seeing what I memorized, and then starting to play up and down what I had memorized to hear it that way. So it’s kind of a weird way of learning how to play, but that’s how I did it. So when I was with Elvin, the changes were not a problem. Then I realized that melody is really your prime source to glean improvisational ideas from. My biggest thing is, listen to somebody play “Straight No Chaser.” Okay? You got that melody [scats] all that chromaticism. The minute the head stops, how many people reference the melody? They go right into their stock way of playing on the blues, but yet there’s that great source there of all that chromatic material. Very few people glean — and that’s a good way to practice. Think of that tune and then solo off that tune, and then go back to playing standard and think about well what does that melody mean?
